name: The Digestive System
what: Covers the structure and function of the human gastrointestinal tract, the roles of accessory organs, the specialised cells of the stomach and small intestine, and the malfunctions of coeliac disease and heartburn.
why: The digestive system illustrates how specialised cells and tissues form organs that cooperate in a system, and it provides concrete examples of absorption, enzyme action and surface area principles that recur across the course.

items.title: I can define the four processes of the digestive system: ingestion, digestion, absorption and egestion
items.what: Ingestion is food entering via the mouth; digestion is the physical and chemical breakdown of food; absorption is the movement of nutrients into the bloodstream; egestion is the removal of undigested waste via the anus.
items.why: These four terms define the overall role of the system and are frequently used as the framework for extended-response answers about digestion.
items.example: When you eat a sandwich, ingestion occurs at the mouth, digestion of starch begins there too, glucose is absorbed through villi in the jejunum, and cellulose fibre is egested as faeces.

items.title: I can distinguish between physical and chemical digestion and give examples of each
items.what: Physical (mechanical) digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing surface area without changing chemical composition. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into absorbable subunits.
items.why: Understanding how these two processes complement each other is essential for explaining why chewing speeds up chemical digestion and for interpreting enzyme pH graphs in exam questions.
items.example: Teeth physically crush bread into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for salivary amylase to chemically break starch into maltose — the enzyme acts faster because more surface is accessible.

items.title: I can describe the role of each organ and accessory organ along the gastrointestinal tract
items.what: The GI tract includes the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) and large intestine. Accessory organs — liver, gall bladder and pancreas — contribute digestive secretions but are not part of the tube itself.
items.why: Identifying structures and their functions is directly tested in short-answer questions, including diagram labelling tasks.
items.example: The pancreas secretes amylase, trypsin and lipase into the duodenum, along with bicarbonate to neutralise acidic chyme arriving from the stomach and restore a pH suitable for these enzymes.

items.title: I can explain the role of the three major classes of digestive enzymes and their substrates and products
items.what: Amylases break polysaccharides (starch) into disaccharides then monosaccharides. Proteases (pepsin, trypsin, peptidases) break proteins into peptides then amino acids. Lipases break fats into glycerol and fatty acid chains.
items.why: Enzyme substrate-product relationships are regularly tested, including questions linking enzyme location to the pH conditions present in that organ.
items.example: Pepsin is active at pH 2–3 in the stomach and cleaves proteins into peptides; trypsin is active at pH 6–8 in the small intestine and continues protein breakdown — their different optimal pH values reflect their different locations.

items.title: I can describe the specialised cells of the stomach and their individual roles
items.what: Four specialised cells line the stomach: goblet cells secrete mucus to protect the lining; parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid; chief cells secrete pepsin; G cells secrete the hormone gastrin, which stimulates acid production.
items.why: This is a specific study design requirement and demonstrates how multiple specialised cell types cooperate within a single organ.
items.example: Goblet cells are essential because without their mucus layer, the hydrochloric acid secreted by parietal cells would digest the stomach wall itself — a failure of this protection leads to gastric ulcers.

items.title: I can explain how the structure of the small intestine maximises nutrient absorption
items.what: The small intestine is approximately 6 m long, highly folded, and lined with villi (0.5–1.6 mm fingerlike projections), each covered in microvilli (~1 µm). Together these features create a total absorptive surface area of approximately 250 m².
items.why: This is a direct application of the SA:V ratio principle and is a high-frequency exam topic, including questions that link villi structure to absorption mechanisms.
items.example: Without villi and microvilli, the internal surface of the small intestine would be roughly the size of a bath towel. With them, it is the size of a tennis court — a roughly 600-fold increase in absorptive area.

items.title: I can explain how different nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine and by what method
items.what: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed into capillaries within villi by facilitated diffusion and active transport. Glycerol and fatty acids, being lipid-soluble, diffuse into lacteals (lymphatic vessels) within villi. Water is absorbed by osmosis.
items.why: Membrane transport mechanisms are linked directly to the digestive system in exam questions, requiring students to specify the method and direction for each nutrient.
items.example: Glucose moves from the jejunum lumen (high concentration after a meal) into the blood (lower concentration) via facilitated diffusion using carrier proteins, then travels via the portal vein to the liver.

items.title: I can describe the cause and consequences of coeliac disease and heartburn
items.what: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition where gluten triggers immune attack on small intestine cells, flattening villi and reducing absorption. Heartburn results from a weakened cardiac sphincter allowing gastric acid into the oesophagus.
items.why: Malfunctions are explicitly required by the study design and test whether students can apply structural knowledge to explain physiological consequences.
items.example: In coeliac disease, flattened villi reduce the absorptive surface area of the small intestine, leading to nutrient deficiencies including iron deficiency anaemia and vitamin D deficiency causing bone weakness.
